chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
title: Leaving the lumber yard for Canadian Jackson's band
summary: Dawson says no one else in his family played; he left a lumber yard when Cornelius Jackson offered work, earned twenty-two dollars the first night, and later ran his own band at Harry Parker's.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Did he play music? No. Anybody in your family play music with you? No. Just me. Not even your children? No. Have you been playing music all your life, like for your own profession?

You had nothing to do, didn't you? I started when, with a guitar, you know, just like I told you, people sometimes, bands used to serenade, you see. They'd go around people's house like that and serenade them late at night, wake them up.

I want to ask... This is the second reel, the second side of Eddie Dawson? Yeah. I wanted to ask you if you had another kind of job for your, how you made your living, if you had a day job too. Or you just play music all the time. No, I didn't do no work. I didn't work at all. Didn't you work for a bank one time? That's after, long after. That's way back. You didn't work in a lumber yard or anything?

Yeah, before I went to the bank, I worked in a lumber yard, uh, Carrie's, uh, lumber yard, uh, on the basin, near the White Bridge there. You worked there a long time? Oh yeah, I worked there a long time. That's where I left from, to play music. Oh yeah? I was working in a lumber yard, in Cornelius Jackson, come back there and I was playing guitar then. This was a long time ago, this was... Yeah, I know, I was, uh, playing, uh, I used to play guitar. When I started, I started going around in the battlefield at night, on the weekend, with that Morton boy, Coochie Morton, Don Morton and them, we'd all get, we'd get Marilyn, guitar and bass, and, and we'd go around and, certain they'd go around, the women liked that, you know, the women used to have fish fries things going on then, you see. There was always something going on on the weekend, right? Saturday night, Saturday night and Sunday. And, uh, so, uh, I was such a good guitar player, I had a way of, uh, without playing a compliment, I could pick. I could play, play a whole lead, a whole number, from the lead, the whole lead of it, on the guitar. So, uh, Kinese come, uh, they got me off the lumber yard and told me, uh, if I wanted to go down and go to Carré, uh, I could make some good money. First, I said, I, I started to hesitate, but I, I couldn't give him my word, so, afterwards, I studied, I said, alright, I'll, I'll go down there with you tonight. So, uh, I went on down there with him that night, and, uh, twenty-two dollars I made the first night. Well, that was big money for me to make, you know, I wasn't used to making that kind of money. I forgot all about the lumber yard then, huh? And every night, well, I was working with him every night, he's a fellow, there's no one that's Canadian Jacks, he used to play the violin. And he'd have a cigarette, he'd be smoking a cigarette, and he'd put it behind his ear, stick the cigarette behind him, they wouldn't point him or nothing. He'd play the violin. Could he sing? Could he sing? Yes, he did, he sang. He'd sing and play the violin at the same time? Yeah, he'd sing and play, at the same time. What did he do with his cigarette when he was singing? Well, he, like, he couldn't do nothing but leave it back there behind his ear, so he'd be true.
A little cigarette. And you just played with him, he had two pieces, just guitar and violin. No, we had a bass, too.

Oh, yeah. Yeah. And, uh, from that on, I just kept on going, and I would work myself on up there, you know, when I found myself, I was, I was at Harry Porphy and Charlie Porphy running my own band then. I got with Marion Vanilla, and, uh, had my own line up there.
